SRAM was fabricated using woven glass fiber reinforced polyester with about 60% fiber volume fraction.
Magnetic absorbing particles were added to the matrix in concentrations from 0 to 20 wt%.
Dynamic compressive tests were conducted using the Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar (SHPB) at strain rates up to 600 s⁻¹.
Compressive strength along the in-plane direction increased from 53.3 MPa (static) to 133.1 MPa at 600 s⁻¹.
Failure strain along the in-plane direction decreased from 0.0194 (static) to 0.0059 at 600 s⁻¹.
At 600 s⁻¹, compressive strength along the normal direction was 349.4 MPa with failure strain of 0.0245, both higher than in-plane values.
Failure under in-plane compression initiates at the fiber-matrix interface due to Poisson ratio mismatch.
Longitudinal splitting, interfacial cracking, and delamination are main fracture modes under dynamic in-plane loading.
Magnetic absorbing particles cause some mechanical property deterioration but do not significantly reduce compressive strength.
Radar absorption tests showed two absorption peaks at 3.2–4 GHz and 11–15 GHz, with 90% absorption of incident waves.
SEM images revealed debonding between fiber and matrix, matrix cracks, and cracks between fiber bundles.
Inhomogeneous distribution of magnetic absorbing particles disrupts matrix continuity and microstructure integrity.
The initial modulus of SRAM is lower than that of neat fiber reinforced composites without absorbing particles.
Under dynamic loading, absorbing particles help support load and inhibit crack propagation.
The addition of absorbing particles improves radar absorbing properties significantly.
Specimens were polished before testing to reduce friction effects in SHPB experiments.
Static compressive tests were performed at a loading rate of 2 mm/min using an INSTRON 1186 machine.
The mismatch of Poisson ratios between glass fiber and polyester matrix causes interfacial shear stress leading to damage.
The study proposes a fracture mechanism explaining the dynamic compressive failure modes of SRAM.
The research fills a gap by focusing on mechanical properties of SRAM, which have been less studied compared to coatings.
